newsitem.title: INDIA: Environmentalists blocking power plants - India PM.
newsitem.headline: Environmentalists blocking power plants - India PM.

text.p: Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda on Wednesday accused environmental activists of standing in the way of India's effort to attract billions of dollars of investment to feed the country's huge appetite for power.

"Some people think that they are born only to protect the environment in this country and God has sent them to this earth only to protect the environment, as if we are not interested in environment," he told a state chief ministers' conference.
Deve Gowda said India needed around 5,000 billion rupees ($140 billion) over the next five years to meet its power generation and distribution needs.

Without explicitly identifying activist groups, he criticised court cases opposing power projects on the grounds that they could harm the environment, and said this resulted in unwanted cost escalations.

"Unfortunately, today, if we clear a project the next day there will be a public interest litigation. Whether it is public interest litigation or political interest litigation, I do not know," Deve Gowda told the conference on power policy.

Opposition parties and environmental activists have been highly critical of proposed power projects undertaken by the private sector, which India has been seeking under an economic reform programme launched in 1991.
Power projects by U.S. firm Enron Corp and Cogentrix have been delayed for years by legal action, as has a multi-billion hydroelectric project on the Narmada river.
"Are those people who are debating, discussing and fighting for the cause of the environment not interested in the development of the country?," Deve Gowda said.
"Without power, can anybody expect industrial growth. Can anybody expect growth in agriculture?," he said in an unprepared speech, which was released later by the government.
Deve Gowda said political parties must bury their differences to enable the necessary investments in the power sector.
"How long can we play this type of mean politics? Let us collectively take a decision today," he said.

Deve Gowda, whose United Front alliance leans heavily on regional political parties, said state governments would be granted more power to approve power projects and and clear environmental objections.
"Why should the state governments come to Delhi? What for?," he said.
